nameStory: The tuberculate dorid gets its name from the small bumps or 'tubercles' that dot its back like tiny pearls. The word 'tuberculate' comes from Latin meaning 'having small swellings,' while 'dorid' refers to this group of sea slugs that carry their gills in a circle around their rear end, named after the sea nymph Doris from Greek mythology.
description: The tuberculate dorid is a small, shell-less sea slug that looks like a tiny, translucent cushion crawling along the ocean floor. These delicate marine creatures are nudibranches (pronounced 'NEW-dih-branks'), which means 'naked gills' - you can actually see their feathery breathing organs protruding from their backs. They're typically whitish or pale yellow with a bumpy texture, growing to about the size of a grape. Like all sea slugs, they're actually snails that have evolved to lose their shells entirely.

idTips.label: Tubercled back surface
idTips.description: The back feels slightly rough to gentle touch, covered in small, rounded bumps that look like tiny beads embedded in jelly

idTips.label: Circular gill arrangement
idTips.description: Feathery, tree-like gills form a perfect circle around the rear opening, retracting instantly when disturbed

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Body appears almost see-through with a pearl-like or milky white coloration, sometimes with pale yellow tints

idTips.label: Two sensory tentacles
idTips.description: A pair of club-shaped tentacles at the head end, often with ridged surfaces that feel slightly textured

idTips.label: Smooth gliding movement
idTips.description: Moves with a flowing, wave-like motion across surfaces, leaving no visible slime trail

habitat: Look for tuberculate dorids in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal waters along New England's coast, especially around tide pools and kelp beds. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found crawling on rocks, seaweed, or the undersides of overhanging ledges where they feed on sponges. You'll have the best luck spotting them in protected coves and among the complex rocky substrates typical of Maine's and Massachusetts' granite coastlines.

seasonality.spring: Most active period as warming waters trigger feeding and reproductive behavior. Look for them during low tides on sunny days when they're easier to spot against wet rocks.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation season when they're most abundant and visible in tide pools. Their translucent bodies are easiest to distinguish against the darker summer growth of seaweeds and algae.
seasonality.fall: Still commonly seen but beginning to move to deeper waters. Often found in larger aggregations as they prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Rarely visible in intertidal zones as they retreat to deeper, more stable waters. Occasionally found under rocks during exceptionally low winter tides.

funFact: Tuberculate dorids are living chemistry labs that steal defensive compounds from the sponges they eat, essentially becoming poisonous by borrowing toxins from their prey - it's like a tiny underwater arms dealer that becomes bulletproof by eating bullets!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small, white sea slugs like the white Atlantic cadlina, but the tuberculate dorid's distinctive bumpy back texture sets it apart - run your finger gently over it and you'll feel those telltale bumps, while smooth-backed species feel like wet silk.
contextualKnowledge: This species has undergone a recent name change from the genus Adalaria to Onchidoris based on DNA studies, so you might see it listed under either name in older field guides. The scientific name shuffle is common in sea slug research as scientists discover these creatures are more closely related than their appearances might suggest.
compareHints: Since this is the only Adalaria species recorded in New England waters, compare it with other members of the onchidoridid family by looking for the characteristic tubercles. Other family members tend to have either completely smooth backs or different bump patterns, making the evenly distributed, bead-like tubercles a reliable family signature. The tuberculate dorid's bumps are also more pronounced and regular than the subtle texturing found on most related species.
